mainTopic: יש אם למקרא and כח כחו; the משנה of the stone-thrower: when גלות applies, ״וּמָצָא״, and אבא שאול's rule that exile is only for an optional activity
overview: The amud opens by defending רבי's ruling about a flying splinter. His spelling-based proof seems to clash with his own view, יש אם למקרא, and the answer is that his word 'ועוד' adds a second proof that does not depend on the spelling. רב פפא then compares dates knocked off a palm tree to the splinter case and shows what a true כח כחו case would be. A new משנה follows. A person who throws a stone into רשות הרבים and kills goes to גלות, unless, according to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, the victim stuck his head out after the stone was thrown. Throwing into one's own courtyard brings גלות only if the victim had permission to be there, which is learned from the forest פסוק. אבא שאול learns from the same פסוק that גלות applies only to an optional activity, so a father, a teacher and a בית דין messenger are exempt. The גמרא explains that the stone-thrower is a שוגג, neither פושע nor אונס, using רב פפא's scrap-heap case, and it explains the word ״וּמָצָא״ from the context of its פסוק. Finally רבא defends אבא שאול's reading that the wood-cutting is רשות. When רב אדא בר אהבה challenges his proof from the word אשר, רבא begins an answer that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: But רבי holds that the reading of the text is what counts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that רבי's view depends on יש אם למסורת, because רבי יוחנן says רבי holds יש אם למקרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רב יצחק son of רבי יוסף say in the name of רבי יוחנן: רבי, רבי יהודה בן רועץ, בית שמאי, רבי שמעון and רבי עקיבא all hold that the way the Torah is read is what counts?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the explanation just given for רבי's ruling. It quotes a list showing that רבי follows the reading of the text, not its spelling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just before this, רב חייא בר אשי explained that רבי's ruling in the splinter case comes from how a word in the פסוק is spelled (יש אם למסורת). But רבי יוחנן clearly lists רבי among those who learn from how the words are read (יש אם למקרא). So the explanation seems to contradict רבי's known approach.

keyTerms.meaning: The way the Torah is read (with its vowels) is the basis for learning
The way the Torah is written (its spelling) is the basis for learning
All of them hold

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two terms. מקרא means how the word is read out loud (the vowels). מסורת means how the letters are written. Some words are written one way and read another.

phrases.english: But didn't Rav Yitzchak son of Rabbi Yosef say
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Rabbi, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz,
phrases.notes: "רבי" with no name means רבי יהודה הנשיא.

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית שַׁמַּאי, וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא,
phrases.english: and Beit Shammai, and Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Akiva,
all of them hold
that the way the text is read is the basis!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב חייא בר אשי's explanation (from just before this section) that רבי relies on יש אם למסורת.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי's ruling in the splinter case is based on יש אם למסורת.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן's list places רבי among those holding יש אם למקרא, so he should not base a ruling on the spelling.

steps.title: That is why רבי said 'and furthermore'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי added a second argument ('ועוד') precisely because his first argument depends on spelling, which he himself may not accept.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is why he said to them: 'And furthermore.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction. רבי gave a spelling-based argument, and then added 'ועוד' with another argument that works even if we follow the reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי's first proof works if we follow the spelling (יש אם למסורת). With the word 'ועוד' he added a second proof that does not depend on the spelling, so it works even by his own view, יש אם למקרא. So there is no contradiction: the spelling argument was not his only basis.

keyTerms.meaning: That is why he said
And furthermore: signals an additional argument

steps.whatToRemember: Even though רבי holds יש אם למקרא, he can bring a spelling-based argument as long as he adds a backup proof ('ועוד') that stands on its own.

phrases.english: That is why he said to them
"And furthermore."
phrases.notes: He's pointing back to the word 'ועוד' in רבי's argument with the רבנן, earlier on the daf.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the speaker's words: the spelling argument is only one of two proofs.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי's ruling rests entirely on יש אם למסורת, which contradicts his known view.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי's 'ועוד' adds a second proof, so his ruling does not depend only on the spelling.

steps.title: Knocking dates off a palm tree is the same dispute
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rules that if someone throws a clod at a palm tree, dates fall and kill someone, this falls under the dispute between רבי and רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Someone who threw a clod of earth at a palm tree and knocked off dates, and the dates went and killed someone — we have arrived at the dispute of רבי and רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא brings a new case and says it matches the earlier dispute about a splinter that flies off wood and kills someone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the splinter case, the person hit one object and a piece of it flew off and killed. רבי says he goes into exile and רבנן exempt him. Here too the thrower hit the tree and dates came off and killed, so רב פפא says it is the same מחלוקת.

keyTerms.meaning: A clod of earth
A palm tree
Dates
We have arrived at the dispute: this case fits an existing מחלוקת

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
one who threw a clod at a palm tree
and knocked off dates,
and the dates went and killed someone,
we have arrived at the dispute of Rabbi and the Rabbis.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the source of רבי's view to applying the dispute to a new case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dates knocked off a tree by a thrown clod are treated like the flying splinter: רבי obligates exile, רבנן exempt.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב פפא needed to say this, since the case looks identical to the splinter case.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא: his case looks exactly like the splinter case, so what is he teaching? This sets up the next step's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אמורא should not be saying something we already know. Since the dates come off the tree just like the splinter comes off the wood, the comparison seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious: a challenge that a statement teaches nothing new

phrases.english: That's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רב פפא's statement teaches anything new.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The case is plainly identical to the splinter case, so stating it seems unnecessary.

steps.title: We might have thought it was a weaker, second-hand force
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we might have thought the falling dates count as כח כחו (a force produced by his force), where even רבי would exempt; רב פפא teaches that it is his direct force.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said it is like 'the force of his force.' So he teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what רב פפא added: the dates are not a second-level force, but count as the thrower's own force.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the splinter, the chopping itself breaks the piece off. With the dates, the clod hits the tree and the dates drop, which might seem one step further away (כח כחו), where even רבי would exempt. רב פפא teaches that this still counts as כחו, his own force, so the מחלוקת applies.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said: introduces a mistaken assumption
The force of his force: an indirect, second-level result of his action
He teaches us (that it is not so)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the line between כחו (his own force), where רבי obligates exile, and כח כחו, where even רבי exempts.

phrases.english: You might have said
that it is like the force of his force,
so he teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifying the new point: ruling out a mistaken classification.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dates falling might count as כח כחו, so even רבי would exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dates count as his direct force, so רבי and רבנן disagree here as in the splinter case.

steps.title: What would count as כח כחו for רבי?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for an example of כח כחו according to רבי, since even the dates case counts as direct force.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, according to רבי, how can you find a case of 'the force of his force'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks: if even falling dates count as direct force, what case would be far enough to be כח כחו for רבי? The answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 assumed that כח כחו exists as a category where even רבי exempts. Since the dates case was pulled into 'direct force', the גמרא wants a concrete example to show the category is real.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you find it? (asks for a real example)

phrases.english: But the force of his force, according to Rabbi,
how can you find it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כֹּחַ כֹּחוֹ לְרַבִּי הֵיכִי מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the category of כח כחו mentioned in step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete case that counts as כח כחו according to רבי.

steps.title: A chain reaction: clod, branch, cluster, dates
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives an example: the clod hits a branch, the branch hits a cluster of dates, and the dates fall and kill.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, he threw a clod and it hit a branch, and the branch went and hit a cluster of dates and knocked off dates, and the dates went and killed someone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a case that has an extra link in the chain. This is כח כחו, where even רבי exempts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב פפא's case the clod knocks dates off directly. Here the clod moves a branch, and it is the branch's movement that knocks off the dates. That extra step makes it the force of his force, not his own force.

keyTerms.meaning: A branch (here, of the palm tree)
A cluster of dates
It struck it

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי: a clod that knocks dates off directly is his force (מחלוקת with רבנן). A clod that moves a branch, which then knocks off the dates, is כח כחו, and he is exempt.

phrases.english: For example, where he threw a clod
and it struck a branch,
and the branch went and struck a cluster of dates
and knocked off dates,
and the dates went and killed someone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A chain where the clod moves a branch, and the branch knocks off the dates that kill, is כח כחו according to רבי.

steps.title: The משנה: throwing a stone into the public area
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that someone who throws a stone into רשות הרבים and kills goes into exile.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who throws a stone into the public domain and kills someone goes into exile.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts. It gives the basic rule: throwing a stone into a public area and killing someone by accident means exile.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה treats this killing as accidental, so the thrower goes to exile. This is the basic rule, and the next step brings a view that limits it. Later, in step 13, the גמרא will ask how throwing into a place where people are around can count as an accident at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין: our משנה
Public domain: a public area where people pass
Goes into exile (to a city of refuge)

phrases.english: Mishnah
One who throws a stone into the public domain
and kills someone, goes into exile.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה, separate from the palm-tree discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Throwing a stone into רשות הרבים and killing someone leads to exile.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב: if the victim stuck his head out afterward
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב rules that if the victim put his head out only after the stone left the thrower's hand, the thrower is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says: If, after the stone left his hand, the other person stuck his head out and got hit, the thrower is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, who limits the rule. If the victim only showed up in the stone's path after it was thrown, the thrower does not go into exile.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key time is the moment of throwing. If nobody was there when the stone was released, and the victim put himself in the way afterward, the thrower is not held responsible with exile.

keyTerms.meaning: That other person (the victim)
Exempt (here, from exile)

steps.whatToRemember: Basic rule: throwing into רשות הרבים and killing means exile. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב: if the victim stuck his head out only after the stone was thrown, the thrower is exempt.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says:
If, after the stone left his hand,
the other person stuck out his head and was hit by it,
he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limiting view to the משנה's basic rule in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the victim entered the stone's path only after it was thrown, the thrower is exempt from exile.

steps.title: Throwing a stone into one's own courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that if someone throws a stone into his own courtyard and kills, he goes to exile only if the victim had the right to be there.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he threw a stone into his own courtyard and killed someone: if the victim was allowed to go in there, the thrower goes to exile; if not, he does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a new case, a stone thrown into the thrower's own private courtyard. The ruling depends on whether the victim was allowed to be there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 8 the stone went into רשות הרבים, where everyone is allowed to be. Now the place is private. So the question becomes whether the victim had a right to be in that courtyard. If he did, the killing counts like any other accident, and the killer goes to exile. If he did not, there is no exile.

keyTerms.meaning: Courtyard; here, the thrower's own private yard
Permission, the right to be somewhere
The one who was harmed; here, the victim
Goes into exile, to an עיר מקלט

phrases.english: If he threw the stone into his courtyard and killed,
if the victim had permission
to enter there, he is exiled,
and if not, he is not exiled,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list of stone-throwing cases, moving from the public domain to a private courtyard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Throwing into one's own courtyard brings exile only if the victim had permission to be there.

steps.title: The forest verse as the source
steps.stepSummary: The משנה proves its courtyard rule from the פסוק about a man going into the forest with his friend. A forest is a place both people may enter.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the פסוק says, 'One who goes with his friend into the forest.' A forest is a place both the victim and the killer may enter. So too, exile applies in any place both may enter. That leaves out a homeowner's courtyard, where both do not have the right to enter.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the פסוק behind the rule we just learned. It uses the forest as the model case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah's example of an accidental killing happens in a forest, where both people have an equal right to be. The משנה takes that as the requirement for exile. So a private courtyard, where the victim had no right to enter, does not lead to exile.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who caused the harm; here, the killer
Forest
Literally 'went out'; this case is left out of the rule
Homeowner

phrases.english: as it is said: 'And one who comes with his neighbor into the forest'
just as the forest is a place where there is permission
for the victim and the one who harms to enter there,
so too, any place where there is permission
for the victim and the one who harms to enter there.
This leaves out the courtyard of the homeowner,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין רְשׁוּת לַנִּיזָּק וְלַמַּזִּיק לִיכָּנֵס לְשָׁם.
phrases.english: where the victim and the one who harms do not both have permission to enter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the courtyard rule in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that exile applies only where both parties had the right to be.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 19:5, the forest case, where both people may enter.

steps.title: אבא שאול: exile only for an optional activity
steps.stepSummary: אבא שאול learns from the same פסוק that exile applies only when the killer was doing something optional, like chopping wood. That leaves out a father, a teacher, and a בית דין messenger.
steps.simpleTranslation: אבא שאול says: chopping wood is optional, so exile applies only to optional activities. That leaves out a father who hits his son, a teacher who disciplines his student, and a messenger of בית דין.
steps.whatsHappening: אבא שאול draws a second lesson from the forest פסוק. He looks at what the man was doing there, which was chopping wood, an activity he did not have to do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Chopping wood is something a person chooses to do. So exile applies only to a killing that happened during a voluntary activity. A father disciplining his son, a teacher disciplining a student, and a בית דין messenger carrying out lashes are all doing a מצוה. If one of them kills by accident, he does not go to exile.

keyTerms.meaning: Chopping wood, the activity in the פסוק
Who disciplines or keeps in line
A messenger of the court, here the one who gives lashes

steps.confusionAlert: The word רְשׁוּת means two different things here. In steps 10 and 11 it means 'permission to be in a place.' For אבא שאול it means 'optional,' something a person was not required to do.
steps.whatToRemember: The forest פסוק gives two limits on exile. Both people must have had the right to be in the place. And, for אבא שאול, the killer must have been doing something optional, not carrying out a מצוה.

phrases.english: Abba Shaul says:
just as chopping wood is optional,
so too, all cases must be optional,
this leaves out the father who hits his son,
and the teacher who disciplines his student,
and the messenger of the court.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a different lesson from the same forest פסוק used in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Exile applies only to a killing during an optional activity. Someone carrying out a מצוה of discipline or punishment is exempt.

steps.title: Throwing into the public domain is deliberate
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה from step 8. Throwing a stone into רשות הרבים, where people are always around, should count as deliberate, not accidental.
steps.simpleTranslation: Into the public domain? He is acting deliberately!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion by attacking the משנה's ruling that throwing into רשות הרבים leads to exile.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Exile is only for an accidental killing. Anyone who throws a stone into a public area knows people are likely to be there. So this seems close to deliberate, and exile would not fit.

keyTerms.meaning: Deliberate, done on purpose or with full awareness

phrases.english: GEMARA: Into the public domain?
He is deliberate!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה in step 8 and challenges it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in step 8 that throwing a stone into רשות הרבים and killing leads to exile.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Throwing into a place full of people is not accidental, so exile should not apply.

steps.title: He was knocking down his wall
steps.stepSummary: רב שמואל בר יצחק answers that the משנה is not talking about simply throwing a stone. It means someone knocking down his wall, whose stones fell into the street.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שמואל בר יצחק said: it is talking about someone knocking down his wall.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא answers the challenge by explaining the case in the משנה more narrowly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Knocking down your own wall is a normal, legitimate activity. If a stone falls into the street, that is far more accidental than throwing a stone there on purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: Knocking down his wall

phrases.english: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak said:
It is about one who is knocking down his wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר יִצְחָק: בְּסוֹתֵר אֶת כּוֹתְלוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 13.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה is about throwing a stone into the street on purpose, which looks deliberate.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about stones falling while someone knocks down his own wall.

steps.title: He should have checked first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: even someone knocking down a wall should check whether anyone is on the other side.
steps.simpleTranslation: He should have checked!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the wall answer. Failing to check is still careless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person knocking down a wall next to a public street knows people pass by. Not looking first is negligence, so it still does not seem accidental enough for exile.

keyTerms.meaning: He should have, he was obligated to
To check, to look carefully

phrases.english: He should have checked!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 14.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Not checking the street before knocking down the wall is negligence, not an accident.

steps.title: He knocked down the wall at night
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that he knocked down the wall at night, when people are rarely in the street.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is about someone knocking down his wall at night.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the case further to fix the problem raised in step 15.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At night the streets are mostly empty. So it is more reasonable that he did not expect anyone to be there.

keyTerms.meaning: At night

phrases.english: It is about one knocking down his wall at night.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 15.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He should have checked because people were around.
steps.terutzMaskana: At night people are rare, so there was little reason to check.

steps.title: Even at night he should check
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the night answer. People can still pass by at night, so he should have checked.
steps.simpleTranslation: At night too he should have checked!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back again. The night answer does not remove the duty to look.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fewer people are around at night, but a public street is never completely empty. So not checking is still careless.

keyTerms.meaning: Also, too

phrases.english: At night too he should have checked!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 16, using the same wording as step 15.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Public streets can have people even at night, so failing to check is still negligence.

steps.title: The wall fell onto a scrap heap
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that he knocked down his wall onto a scrap heap, a public spot where people are not normally expected.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is about someone knocking down his wall onto a scrap heap.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a third case: the stones fall onto a garbage heap, not onto a street.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A scrap heap is public in the sense that no one owns it, but people do not usually stand there. So he had no clear reason to expect anyone, yet it is not completely beyond his control either.

keyTerms.meaning: A scrap heap or garbage dump

phrases.english: It is about one knocking down his wall onto a scrap heap.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to a different location
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any public place requires checking, even at night.
steps.terutzMaskana: A scrap heap is a place where people are not normally expected.

steps.title: The scrap heap dilemma
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what kind of scrap heap this is. If people go there often, he is negligent. If they do not, he is completely blameless. Either way, exile does not fit.
steps.simpleTranslation: What kind of scrap heap is this? If many people go there, he is negligent. If many people do not go there, he is completely blameless!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the scrap heap answer with an either-or argument. Both options seem to rule out exile.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Exile is for the middle level of fault: careless, but not reckless. If people often use the heap, he was reckless for not checking. If people never go there, nothing could have been expected of him, so he is fully excused. The גמרא is asking where the middle ground is.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What does it look like?
Are commonly found, often go there
Negligent, reckless
Forced by circumstances, completely blameless

steps.whyThisMatters: This either-or shows the exact zone where exile applies. It is not for reckless behavior and not for an accident that was completely unavoidable. It is only for the middle, real carelessness.

phrases.english: This scrap heap, what is its situation?

phrases.aramaic: אִי שְׁכִיחִי בַּהּ רַבִּים – פּוֹשֵׁעַ הוּא,
phrases.english: If many people are commonly there, he is negligent,

phrases.aramaic: אִי לָא שְׁכִיחִי בַּהּ רַבִּים – אָנוּס הוּא!
phrases.english: if many people are not commonly there, he is completely blameless!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the scrap heap answer in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The scrap heap answer in step 18.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Either people go there and he is reckless, or they do not and he is fully excused. Neither one is the middle-level carelessness that brings exile.

steps.title: A scrap heap used at night and only sometimes by day
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the case is a scrap heap people use at night but only occasionally use by day. The wall-demolisher is neither negligent nor blameless, so גלות fits.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: The case is a scrap heap that people use as a bathroom at night but not usually during the day, though sometimes someone does sit there during the day. He is not negligent, because people do not normally use it during the day. He is also not blameless, because sometimes someone does sit there.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the 'either way' question from step 19 by describing a middle case. This scrap heap is used regularly at night and only now and then during the day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 19 said that a scrap heap is either busy, which makes him a פושע, or empty, which makes him an אונס. רב פפא finds a third option. Since daytime use is not the norm, he is not a פושע. Since it does happen, he should have thought of it, so he is not an אונס either. That leaves him in the middle category of שוגג, which is exactly what גלות needs.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for… (introduces the exact case where a ruling applies)
Scrap heap / garbage dump
Negligent; carelessness close to deliberate
Something beyond one's control; completely blameless
To relieve oneself

steps.whatToRemember: גלות is only for the middle zone. If the harm was very likely (פושע), גלות is too little. If the harm was unforeseeable (אונס), there is no guilt at all. רב פפא's scrap heap sits right in that middle.
steps.whyThisMatters: This defines what שוגג means for גלות: a real but uncommon chance of harm that a careful person would have kept in mind.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: It is only needed
phrases.notes: He means the ruling about the wall-demolisher who goes to גלות only applies in the following case.

phrases.english: for a scrap heap that is commonly used
for relieving oneself there at night,
but is not commonly used for relieving oneself there during the day,
yet there are those who happen to sit there.
He is not negligent –

phrases.aramaic: דְּהָא אֵינָהּ עֲשׂוּיָה לִיפָּנוֹת בָּהּ בַּיּוֹם,
phrases.english: since it is not commonly used for relieving oneself during the day;
he is also not a victim of circumstance,
since there are those who happen to sit there.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לָא צְרִיכָא אֶלָּא לְאַשְׁפָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'either way' challenge of step 19 by finding a middle case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the case more narrowly (a middle-ground scenario)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A scrap heap must be either busy (פושע) or empty (אונס), so גלות could never apply.
steps.terutzMaskana: A scrap heap used at night and only sometimes by day makes him a שוגג, so he goes to גלות.

steps.title: ״וּמָצָא״ excludes someone who puts himself in the stone's path
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי אליעזר בן יעקב from the משנה and brings a ברייתא. The word ״וּמָצָא״ excludes a victim who moved into the path of the stone after it was thrown.
steps.simpleTranslation: Back to the משנה: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says… The רבנן taught: 'And it finds' excludes someone who presents himself. From here רבי אליעזר בן יעקב said: If, after the stone left the thrower's hand, the other person stuck out his head and was hit, the thrower is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to a new line of the משנה, the opinion of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. It brings a ברייתא showing where his ruling comes from in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says the iron 'finds' its victim, which suggests the victim was already there when the throw began. If the victim moved into the path only after the stone was released, the stone did not 'find' him; he came to it. So the thrower is פטור from גלות.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And it finds' (דברים 19:5): the iron finds the victim
To exclude; this word leaves out a certain case
One who presents himself, putting himself in harm's way
Exempt (here, from גלות)

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר וְכוּ׳.
phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov says, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the start of his line in the משנה: if the victim stuck out his head after the stone was thrown, the thrower is exempt.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: "And it finds" –
excluding one who presents himself.

phrases.aramaic: מִכָּאן אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב:
phrases.english: From here Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov said:
If, after the stone left his hand,

phrases.aramaic: הוֹצִיא הַלָּה אֶת רֹאשׁוֹ וְקִבְּלָהּ, פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: the other person stuck out his head and received it, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר וְכוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ״וּמָצָא״ means the victim was already present, so a victim who moves into the stone's path after the throw exempts the thrower.

steps.title: Contradiction: ״וּמָצָא״ by redeeming a field means something found later
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: does ״מָצָא״ really mean 'there from the start'? In the laws of redeeming a field, ״וּמָצָא״ means money that comes later, not property he already had.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean that 'finds' refers to something there from the beginning? But we can point out a contradiction: 'And finds' excludes what was already available. He may not sell a far-away field to redeem a nearby one, or sell a poor field to redeem a good one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reading in step 21. It brings another ברייתא in which the same word ״וּמָצָא״ is read the opposite way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: About redeeming a sold ancestral field, the פסוק says 'and he finds enough for its redemption' (ויקרא 25:26). The ברייתא there says this excludes money from land he already owned at the time of the first sale. In that case ״מָצָא״ means something new that appears later, which contradicts step 21's 'there from the start'.

keyTerms.meaning: Does this mean to say…? (introduces a questioning inference)
From the beginning; already present beforehand
And they pointed out a contradiction (two sources seem to clash)
Already available; something he had on hand
And redeem (buying back an ancestral field)

steps.confusionAlert: The two ברייתות do not argue about גלות. The question is only about the meaning of the same word ״וּמָצָא״ in two different פסוקים.

phrases.english: Is that to say that "finds" implies from the beginning?
But raise a contradiction: "And finds" – excluding what was already available,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:26, about someone buying back the field he sold.

phrases.english: that he may not sell a distant field and redeem a nearby one,
or sell a poor field and redeem a good one!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading of ״וּמָצָא״ used in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that ״מָצָא״ means 'already there from the start'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another ברייתא reads the same word as 'newly found later', so one word seems to get two opposite meanings.

steps.title: Each ״וּמָצָא״ is read by the context of its own פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the context decides. By redeeming a field, ״וּמָצָא״ goes with 'his hand attains', which means from now on. By גלות, ״וּמָצָא״ goes with 'the forest', which was there from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Here we learn from the context of the פסוק, and there we learn from the context of the פסוק. There, 'and finds' is like 'and his hand attains'. Just as 'his hand attains' means from now on, so 'finds' means from now on. Here, 'and finds' is like the forest. Just as a forest is something there from the start, so 'finds' means something there from the start.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא resolves the contradiction from step 22. The word itself is flexible, and each פסוק's surrounding words tell us which meaning it has.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the field פסוק, ״וּמָצָא״ comes right after 'his hand attains', which is clearly new money. Had he had money before, he would not have sold his field. So ״מָצָא״ there also means newly found. In the גלות פסוק the scene is a forest, which exists before the accident. So ״מָצָא״ there means the victim was already present.

keyTerms.meaning: From the context of the פסוק
Similar to; read like the neighboring words
'And his hand attains' (ויקרא 25:26): he gets new means
From now; newly
Forest (the setting of the accident in דברים 19:5)

steps.whatToRemember: The same word can mean different things in different פסוקים. Context decides. By גלות, ״וּמָצָא״ means the victim was already there, which is why רבי אליעזר בן יעקב exempts the thrower when the victim moves into the path later.

phrases.english: Rava said: Here it is from the context of the verse
and there it is from the context of the verse.
There, from the context of the verse:
phrases.notes: "There" is the פסוק about buying back a field.

phrases.english: "and finds" is like "and his hand attains,"
just as "his hand attains" is from now,
so too "finds" is also from now.
Here, from the context of the verse:
"and finds" is like the forest,
just as a forest is something that exists from the beginning,
so too "and finds" also refers to something that exists from the beginning.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הָכָא מֵעִנְיָינֵיהּ דִּקְרָא וְהָתָם מֵעִנְיָינֵיהּ דִּקְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Context-based reading: each פסוק's surrounding words decide what the word means
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ״וּמָצָא״ must have one fixed meaning everywhere, so the two ברייתות contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: By the field, ״מָצָא״ means newly found (like 'his hand attains'). By גלות, it means already present (like the forest).

steps.title: Maybe the wood-cutting in the פסוק is for a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: Back on the משנה of the stone-thrower, a scholar asks רבא how we know the wood-cutting in the forest is optional. Maybe it is for a סוכה or for the altar, and the Torah still says he goes to גלות.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: one who throws a stone, etc. One of the Sages said to רבא: How do you know the forest case is about cutting wood for an optional purpose? Maybe it is wood cut for a סוכה, or wood for the altar fire, and even so the Torah says he is exiled!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה, where אבא שאול learns that גלות is only for someone doing an optional act. A scholar challenges this: maybe the wood-cutting in the פסוק is a מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אבא שאול's rule depends on reading the forest case as רשות (optional). If the wood was being cut for a מצוה like a סוכה or the מערכה on the altar, the Torah would be sending a מצוה-doer to גלות. Then the exemption for מצוה cases would fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: cutting (chopping) wood
optional, not a מצוה
the booth built for the holiday of סוכות
the arranged woodpile burning on the altar
'the Merciful One', meaning the Torah or ה׳

phrases.english: One who throws the stone, etc.
One of the Sages said to Rava:
From where do we know it is from cutting wood that is optional?
Perhaps it is from cutting wood for a sukka,
or from cutting wood for the altar pile,
and even so the Merciful One said: let him be exiled!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section on a later line of the משנה (אבא שאול's derivation).
steps.kashyaTarget: אבא שאול's reading that the forest wood-cutting is רשות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק never says the cutting is optional. It could be for a מצוה, which would mean even מצוה-doers go to גלות.

steps.title: Cutting wood is never itself a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that if the wood were already cut, nobody would cut more. So the act of cutting is not the מצוה, even when there is no cut wood available.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: Since if he found wood already cut he would not cut, cutting is not a מצוה. So now too, when he does cut, it is not a מצוה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends אבא שאול. The cutting is only a means to get wood, so the cutting itself is optional.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מצוה is to have a סוכה or a woodpile, not to chop. The proof: if ready-cut wood is around, there is no reason to chop at all. Chopping is just preparation, so it counts as רשות.

keyTerms.meaning: already cut
it is not a מצוה
now too, in this case as well

phrases.english: He said to him:
Since if he found it already cut
he does not cut, it is not a מצוה;
now too, it is not a מצוה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the act: the cutting is only preparation for a מצוה, not a מצוה itself.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Cutting wood for a סוכה or the altar is a מצוה act.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since cut wood would make chopping unnecessary, chopping is always רשות.

steps.title: By that logic, a father hitting his son is not a מצוה either
steps.stepSummary: רבינא challenges רבא from the משנה, which exempts a father who hits his son. By רבא's logic, if the son were already learned there would be no hitting, so the hitting should not count as a מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא raised an objection to רבא: The משנה excludes a father who strikes his son, a teacher who disciplines his student, and a court agent. Let us say: since if the son were already learned it would not be a מצוה to hit him, now too it is not a מצוה!
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא turns רבא's reasoning against a case the משנה clearly exempts from גלות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה exempts the father because his hitting is a מצוה. But hitting is only a means toward teaching, just like chopping is only a means toward wood. If 'means to a מצוה' is not a מצוה, the father should go to גלות, which goes against the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: who disciplines or punishes
an agent of the court who carries out lashes
learned, already educated

phrases.english: Ravina raised an objection to Rava:
Excluded is the father who strikes his son,
and the teacher who disciplines his student,
and the agent of the court.

phrases.aramaic: לֵימָא: כֵּיוָן דְּאִילּוּ גְּמִיר לָאו מִצְוָה,
phrases.english: Let us say: since if he were learned it would not be a מצוה,
now too, it is not a מצוה!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's reasoning from step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's rule that a means to a מצוה is not itself a מצוה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Apply the same reasoning to the father, and he should be liable for גלות. That goes against the משנה.

steps.title: Disciplining a son is a מצוה even when he is learned
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the father case is different. Disciplining a son is a מצוה even if he is learned, based on the פסוק 'Chastise your son'.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, even if the son is learned, it is still a מצוה, as it is written: 'Chastise your son and he will give you rest, and he will give delight to your soul.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers רבינא. Hitting a son is not just a tool for learning; a פסוק in משלי makes discipline itself a מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's logic only works when the act stops being needed once the goal is reached, like chopping when wood is already cut. Disciplining a son never becomes unneeded, because the פסוק commands it in its own right. So the father's case is truly a מצוה.

keyTerms.meaning: discipline, chastise
delights

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם אַף עַל גַּב דִּגְמִיר מִצְוָה,
phrases.english: There, even though he is learned, it is a מצוה,
as it is written:
"Chastise your son, and he will give you rest;
and he will give delight to your soul."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's challenge in step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: a פסוק makes the act a מצוה in itself.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Hitting a son is only a means toward teaching, like chopping wood.
steps.terutzMaskana: Discipline is a מצוה on its own, even for a learned son, so the father is exempt.

steps.title: רבא drops his first proof and brings one from 'אשר'
steps.stepSummary: רבא takes back his earlier reasoning. He proves instead that the forest is optional: the פסוק describes a forest a person can enter or not enter as he wishes, and a מצוה would not allow skipping it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא then said: What I said is nothing. The פסוק says, 'And as when one goes with his neighbor into the forest.' A forest is a place where, if he wants, he goes in, and if he wants, he does not. If you think it is a מצוה, could he just choose not to go in?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא withdraws his first answer and gives a new answer to the question of step 24.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new proof comes from the wording of the פסוק itself. It describes going into the forest as something a person may or may not do. A מצוה cannot be skipped, so the case must be רשות.

keyTerms.meaning: it is nothing; it does not hold up
forest
if he wants
it is enough, it is acceptable

phrases.english: Rava then said:
What I said is nothing.
"And as when one goes with his neighbor into the forest,"
phrases.notes: דברים 19:5. The next step shows that רבא's point rests on the word אשר.

phrases.english: what is a forest? One where, if he wants, he enters
and if he wants, he does not enter.
And if it enters your mind that it is a מצוה,
would it be enough for him not to enter?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲדַר אָמַר רָבָא לָאו מִילְּתָא הִיא דַּאֲמַרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבא replaces his answer from step 25 with a new proof.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The forest case is רשות, because the פסוק describes entering as up to the person's choice, which cannot be true of a מצוה.

steps.title: Does 'אשר' always mean 'if he wants'?
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה challenges רבא: does אשר always mean a choice? The impure person who enters the מקדש is also described with אשר. Would someone who became impure burying a מת מצוה, where he had no choice, then be exempt?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה said to רבא: Wherever 'אשר' is written, does it mean 'if he wants'? If so, 'And a man who becomes impure and does not purify himself' would mean only when he chose to become impure. But with a מת מצוה, where he must become impure, would you say he is exempt too?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אדא בר אהבה attacks רבא's new proof by testing the word אשר on a different פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If אשר means 'only by choice', then the כרת for entering the מקדש while impure would apply only to someone who chose to become impure. A person who became impure by burying a מת מצוה had no choice, yet it is hard to say he is exempt. So אשר cannot mean 'optional' everywhere.

keyTerms.meaning: 'who' or 'when'; the word רבא built his proof on
but now, if so (introduces an unacceptable result)
purify himself
an unattended corpse that anyone finding it must bury
exempt

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה לְרָבָא:
phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava said to Rava:
Wherever "asher" is written,
is it a case of "if he wants"?
If that is so,
"And a man who becomes impure and does not purify himself"
phrases.notes: במדבר 19:20. This פסוק gives כרת to someone who enters the מקדש while impure.

phrases.aramaic: אִי בָּעֵי מִיטַּמֵּא אִי בָּעֵי לָא מִיטַּמֵּא.
phrases.english: would mean: if he wants he becomes impure, if he wants he does not.

phrases.aramaic: מֵת מִצְוָה, דְּלָא סַגִּי דְּלָא מִיטַּמֵּא,
phrases.english: With a met מצוה, where it is not possible for him not to become impure,
would you say that he is exempt too?

steps.triggerLanguage: כֹּל הֵיכָא דִּכְתִיב אֲשֶׁר דְּאִי בָּעֵי הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's new proof from step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's reading that אשר means the act is optional
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Use the same reading of אשר in במדבר 19:20, and someone made impure by a מת מצוה would be exempt from כרת, which is hard to accept.

steps.title: The impure person's case is different because of a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבא begins answering רב אדא בר אהבה: the case of the impure person is different, because a special פסוק says something about it. The פסוק itself comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: There it is different, because the verse says:
steps.whatsHappening: רבא starts his answer to the question about the impure person by saying that case is special. He is setting up a פסוק, which the גמרא quotes at the start of the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא does not give up his rule that אשר means a choice. Instead he says the impure person is an exception: a separate פסוק covers that case. So the impure person's law comes from that other פסוק, not from the word אשר, and the proof about the forest can still stand.

keyTerms.meaning: There it is different: the case being compared has a special reason of its own
Because the verse says: introduces a פסוק as the source for the point

steps.confusionAlert: This line is only the opening of רבא's answer. The actual פסוק that explains the difference is quoted at the start of the next amud, so do not expect the full answer here.

phrases.english: There it is different,
phrases.notes: "There" means the impure person who enters the מקדש, the case רב אדא בר אהבה just raised.

phrases.english: because the verse says:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins רבא's answer to רב אדא בר אהבה's challenge from Step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the impure person is set apart by a separate פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the impure person is also described with אשר, אשר cannot always mean a choice, and a person forced to become impure while burying a מת מצוה would be exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: The impure person has its own special פסוק, so that case is no proof against reading אשר as a choice in the forest case.
